edits.before: <para id="import-auto-id1166991830004">The magnetic field of a long straight wire has more implications than you might at first suspect. <emphasis effect="italics">Each segment of current produces a magnetic field like that of a long straight wire, and the total field of any shape current is the vector sum of the fields due to each segment.</emphasis> The formal statement of the direction and magnitude of the field due to each segment is called the <term id="import-auto-id1166991830010">Biot-Savart law</term>. Integral calculus is needed to sum the field for an arbitrary shape current. This results in a more complete law, called <term id="import-auto-id1166991831547">Ampere’s law</term>, which relates magnetic field and current in a general way. Ampere’s law in turn is a part of <link id="import-auto-id1166991831551" document="m52443" target-id="canonical-maxwell-s-equations">Maxwell’s equations</link>, which give a complete theory of all electromagnetic phenomena. Considerations of how Maxwell’s equations appear to different observers led to the modern theory of relativity, and the realization that electric and magnetic fields are different manifestations of the same thing. Most of this is beyond the scope of this text in both mathematical level, requiring calculus, and in the amount of space that can be devoted to it. But for the interested student, and particularly for those who continue in physics, engineering, or similar pursuits, delving into these matters further will reveal descriptions of nature that are elegant as well as profound. In this text, we shall keep the general features in mind, such as RHR-2 and the rules for magnetic field lines listed in Magnetic Fields and Magnetic Field Lines, while concentrating on the fields created in certain important situations.</para>
edits.after: <para id="import-auto-id1166991830004">Each small segment of a steady current contributes to the magnetic field. The <term id="import-auto-id1166991830010">Biot-Savart law</term> gives the size and direction of that contribution; adding the contributions from all segments gives the total field. <term id="import-auto-id1166991831547">Ampere’s law</term> provides another relationship: for steady currents, the accumulated component of the magnetic field along a closed path is proportional to the net current passing through a surface bounded by that path. This is especially useful for highly symmetric current arrangements. Maxwell later extended this law to include changing electric fields, as discussed in <link id="import-auto-id1166991831551" document="m52443">Maxwell’s Equations: Electromagnetic Waves Predicted and Observed</link>.</para>
